title: Noun Declension Classes and Gender in the Nominative
subtitle: Recognizing grammatical gender and primary nominative endings
keyPoint: Lithuanian nouns are grammatically masculine or feminine, identifiable in the nominative singular by endings like -as, -is, -ys for masculine and -a, -ė for feminine.

mistakes.note: Adjectives must match feminine nouns with feminine endings like '-a'.
The noun 'kava' ends in -a and is feminine, requiring the feminine predicate adjective 'šalta'.
The noun 'namas' is masculine, so it requires the masculine adjective 'didelis'.

quiz.question: Identify the masculine noun in the list:
quiz.explanation: Nouns ending in '-as' such as 'berniukas' (boy) are masculine.

quiz.question: Choose the correct adjective form: 'Graž___ mergaitė šypsosi.'
quiz.explanation: 'Mergaitė' is feminine, so the matching adjective ending is '-a' (graži/graža -> graži or regular -a base: 'graži'). Here 'graži' matches 'i' stem, for regular: 'gera'.

quiz.question: Which of these words is a feminine noun ending in '-ė'?
quiz.explanation: 'Upė' (river) ends in '-ė' and belongs to the primary feminine declension pattern.

quiz.question: Select the proper agreement: 'Mano tėvas yra ___.'
quiz.explanation: 'Tėvas' is masculine singular nominative, requiring 'geras'.

tip: Almost all native Lithuanian nouns ending in -as, -is, or -ys are masculine, while nearly everything ending in -a or -ė is feminine.

title: Present Tense Conjugation Groups (-a, -i, -o)
subtitle: Conjugating verbs in the present using 3rd-person reference vowels
keyPoint: Lithuanian present-tense verbs group into three conjugations determined by the 3rd person singular/plural vowel: -a (1st), -i (2nd), or -o (3rd).

mistakes.note: The 3rd-person forms (jis, ji, jie, jos) do not take personal plural endings like -me; they use the bare stem 'dirba'.
The 1st person singular 'aš' takes the ending -u or -au, never the 3rd-person stem vowel alone.
'Turėti' belongs to the 2nd conjugation (-i-), so 'mes' takes the ending '-ime' (turime).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Aš kasdien ___ kavą.' (gerti)
quiz.explanation: 'Aš' takes the ending '-u', making the form 'geriu'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Jie Vilniuje ___.' (gyventi)
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person plural 'jie' uses the base 3rd person form 'gyvena'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Mes ___ lietuviškai.' (kalbėti)
quiz.explanation: For 1st person plural 'mes', verbs take '-me', yielding 'kalbame'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct form for 'tu' with the verb 'mylėti' (to love):
quiz.explanation: 'Tu' for 2nd conjugation takes '-i', resulting in 'myli'.

tip: In Lithuanian, the 3rd-person verb form is unique: singular (jis/ji) and plural (jie/jos) share the EXACT same verb form!

title: Accusative Case for Direct Objects
subtitle: Marking targets of transitive verbs and destinations
keyPoint: The accusative case marks the direct object of an affirmative sentence, typically ending with a nasal vowel letter like -ą, -į, -ų, or -ę in the singular.

mistakes.note: Direct objects of affirmative verbs must take the accusative case with nasal vowels (-ią, -ę).
'Duona' is in the nominative; direct object position requires the accusative ending '-ą'.
'Pienas' must take the accusative masculine singular ending '-ą'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Tomas rašo ___.' (laiškas)
quiz.explanation: The accusative singular for masculine -as nouns ends in '-ą' (laišką).

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Mama verda skanią ___.' (sriuba)
quiz.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in '-a' become '-ą' in the accusative singular.

quiz.question: Choose the correct accusative form of 'katė':
quiz.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in '-ė' change to '-ę' in the accusative singular.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Aš matau gerą ___.' (draugas)
quiz.explanation: 'Draugas' changes to 'draugą' to serve as the direct object in the accusative singular.

tip: Singular accusative nouns always end in a vowel with a tail (ogonek: ą, ę, į, ų), making them easy to spot.

title: Genitive Case for Possession, Absence, and Numbers
subtitle: Expressing belonging, 'of', counted quantities, and non-existence
keyPoint: The genitive case expresses possession, quantity after numbers greater than nine, and non-existence after 'nėra'.

useCases.label: Counted items from 10 to 20 and multiples of ten

mistakes.note: The negative existence word 'nėra' strictly requires the genitive case, not nominative.
Numbers from 10 upwards govern the genitive plural (ending in -ų), not singular.
Possession must be marked by the genitive ending ('brolio') and usually precedes the owned noun.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Lentynoje nėra ___.' (knyga)
quiz.explanation: 'Nėra' requires genitive singular 'knygos'.

quiz.question: Complete the phrase: 'Čia yra Petro ___.' (namas - meaning 'Peter's house')
quiz.explanation: The owner is in the genitive ('Petro'), but the item possessed ('namas') is the subject in nominative.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Mes turime dvidešimt ___.' (studentas)
quiz.explanation: Numerals from 10 to 20 govern the genitive plural, which always ends in '-ų'.

quiz.question: Select the correct form: 'Stiklinė ___.' (sultys - glass of juice)
quiz.explanation: The partitive construction requires the genitive plural form 'sulčių'.

tip: Whenever you express 'someone's' belonging, put that person in the genitive and place them BEFORE the noun they own (e.g., 'Jono raktas' = John's key).

title: The Genitive of Negation
subtitle: Switching direct objects from accusative to genitive in negative sentences
keyPoint: Whenever a transitive verb is negated with the prefix ne-, its direct object obligatorily changes from the accusative to the genitive case.

cells: I read / do not read a book
I drink / do not drink milk
I buy / do not buy apples
I see / do not see friends

mistakes.note: Negation forces the object from accusative (kavą) into genitive (kavos), not nominative.
Learners often mistakenly leave the object in the accusative ('brolį') despite the negative verb.
'Problema' in a negated clause must shift to the genitive singular 'problemos'.

quiz.question: Transform to negative: 'Aš skaitau knygą.' -> 'Aš neskaitau ___.'
quiz.explanation: The accusative 'knygą' becomes genitive 'knygos' when the verb is negated.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Tomas neturi ___.' (automobilis)
quiz.explanation: With the negative verb 'neturi', the direct object takes genitive singular 'automobilio'.

quiz.question: Choose the correct sentence:
quiz.explanation: 'Obuolio' is the genitive form required by the negated verb 'nevalgau'.

quiz.question: Fill in the blank: 'Mes nematom šių ___.' (namai - plural)
quiz.explanation: Plural direct objects shift into the genitive plural ending in '-ų' under negation.

tip: Remember: Positive action = Accusative target; Negative action (ne-) = Genitive target. It is one of the most consistent rules in Lithuanian grammar!

title: Locative Case for Static Position
subtitle: Expressing 'in', 'on', or 'at' using noun endings alone
keyPoint: Lithuanian expresses static location without prepositions by adding locative endings directly to noun stems.

cells: in the city / in the room

mistakes.note: Do not use the preposition 'į' (which takes the accusative and indicates direction into) for static location; use the bare locative.
Static position requires the locative ending '-oje' for feminine nouns ending in '-a', not the nominative form.
The bare locative means 'in'; to express 'on a surface', use the preposition 'ant' with the genitive case.

quiz.question: Jonas dabar gyvena ___ (Vilnius).
quiz.explanation: Proper place names ending in -ius take the locative ending -iuje to denote static location.

quiz.question: Mano sesuo mokosi ___ (universitetas).
quiz.explanation: Masculine nouns ending in -as take the locative ending -e.

quiz.question: Vaikai linksmai žaidžia ___ (kiemas).
quiz.explanation: Kiemas (yard) is a masculine noun ending in -as, so its locative form is kieme.

quiz.question: Ar tavo mama dabar yra ___ (virtuvė)?
quiz.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in -ė take the locative ending -ėje.

tip: Remember that Lithuanian almost never uses prepositions for 'in'; if you mean 'inside' a place or city, the bare locative ending handles the entire job.

title: Instrumental Case with and without 'su'
subtitle: Distinguishing instruments and transport from accompaniment
keyPoint: Use the bare instrumental case for tools, means, and transportation, but add the preposition 'su' when expressing accompaniment.

useCases.label: Social Accompaniment
useCases.example: Vakare einu į kiną su broliu.

mistakes.note: Do not use 'su' for means of transport; transportation uses the bare instrumental.
Tools and instruments take the bare instrumental without 'su'.
Accompaniment ('together with someone') requires the preposition 'su'.

quiz.question: Mes važiuojame į Kauną ___ (automobilis).
quiz.explanation: Means of transportation take the bare instrumental case without any preposition.

quiz.question: Vakar ilgai kalbėjausi ___ (draugas).
quiz.explanation: Accompaniment with people requires the preposition 'su' followed by the instrumental form.

quiz.question: Vaikas piešia gražų namą ___ (pieštukas).
quiz.explanation: A tool or instrument used to perform an action takes the bare instrumental.

quiz.question: Ryte visada geriu kavą ___ (pienas).
quiz.explanation: When an ingredient accompanies another, 'su' + instrumental is required.

tip: Ask yourself: Is this a tool/vehicle I am using, or a companion/addition? If it's a tool or vehicle, drop 'su' entirely.

title: Dative Case and Impersonal Experiencer Constructions
subtitle: Marking recipients and subjects of physical or mental states
keyPoint: The dative marks both the recipient of an action and the experiencer in impersonal state constructions like 'man šalta' or 'man reikia'.

cells: I am cold / I am hot
My daughter is ten years old
I give a flower to my friend

mistakes.note: In Lithuanian, physical sensations use impersonal dative constructions ('Man šalta'), not the nominative pronoun with 'būti'.
The modal word 'reikia' requires the person who needs something to be in the dative case ('man').
'Patikti' (to please/appeal) takes the dative experiencer: literally, 'This book pleases to me'.

quiz.question: ___ (Aš) šiandien labai skauda galvą.
quiz.explanation: Pain and physical conditions take the experiencer in the dative case (man).

quiz.question: Ar ___ (tu) reikia naujo žodyno?
quiz.explanation: 'Reikia' requires the person experiencing the need to be in the dative case (tau).

quiz.question: Gydytojas davė vaistų sergančiam ___ (vaikas).
quiz.explanation: The recipient of the medicine takes the masculine singular dative ending -ui.

quiz.question: ___ (Mes) patinka keliauti po Europą.
quiz.explanation: With the verb 'patikti', the person who likes something must be in the dative case (mums).

tip: Whenever you describe how someone feels (hot, cold, boring, interesting) or what they need, switch the subject pronoun to its dative form (man, tau, jam, jai, mums, jums, jiems, joms).

title: Simple Past Tense with -o and -ė Stems
subtitle: Navigating Lithuanian past tense endings and vowel alternations
keyPoint: The simple past tense in Lithuanian conjugates using either an -o stem or an -ė stem, which must be learned as a principal part alongside the infinitive.

useCases.label: Sequential Past Narratives
useCases.example: Jis grįžo namo, pavalgė ir užmigo.

examples.en: Vakar aš visą dieną sunkiai dirbau.

mistakes.note: Do not construct past tense with an auxiliary verb like in English compound tenses; use the inflected simple past 'mačiau'.
In -ė stems, dental consonants 't' and 'd' mutate before '-iau': 't' becomes 'č' (mačiau), and 'd' becomes 'dž' (sėdėjau -> sėdėjau / vedžiau).

mistakes.wrong: Vakar mes dirbome su -ė galūne: dirbėme.
mistakes.note: The verb 'dirbti' belongs to the -o stem past family (dirbo), so 1st person plural is 'dirbome', not 'dirbėme'.

quiz.question: Praėjusią vasarą mes ___ (būti) prie jūros.
quiz.explanation: The past stem for būti is buvo; the 1st person plural (mes) ending is -ome (buvome).

quiz.question: Aš vakar ___ (matyti) tavo brolį bibliotekoje.
quiz.explanation: The 1st person singular past of matyti is mačiau (with dental mutation t -> č before -iau).

quiz.question: Ką jūs vakar ___ (veikti) vakare?
quiz.explanation: Veikti uses the past stem veikė; the 2nd person plural ending for -ė stems is -ėte (veikėte).

quiz.question: Jonas ir Tomas vakar kartu ___ (sportuoti).
quiz.explanation: Third-person past verbs use the bare stem without a personal suffix: sportavo (both singular and plural).

tip: Always learn Lithuanian verbs as a trio: infinitive, present 3rd person, past 3rd person (e.g., matyti, mato, matė). The 3rd person past stem reveals whether you conjugate with -o or -ė.

title: Frequentative Past Tense (-davo)
subtitle: Expressing habitual, repetitive past actions with the suffix -dav-
keyPoint: The frequentative past expresses repeated or habitual actions in the past and is formed systematically by replacing the infinitive ending -ti with -davo.

useCases.label: Past Childhood Habits
useCases.example: Vaikystėje dažnai žaisdavau lauke su draugais.

useCases.label: Regular Past Routines
useCases.example: Senelis kiekvieną rytą gerdavo juodą kavą.

useCases.label: Recurring Historic Practices
useCases.example: Vasarą mes visada važiuodavome pas močiutę.

examples.en: Mano seneliai anksčiau kaimynams dažnai padėdavo.
Ar tu jaunystėje sportuodavai kiekvieną dieną?
Mes visada kartu pietaudavome šioje kavinėje.

mistakes.note: Rather than translating English 'I used to read' with wordy constructions, Lithuanian uses the concise -dav- frequentative past form.
Do not use the frequentative past for one-off actions that happened once at a specific time; use the simple past instead.
Drop the entire infinitive suffix '-ti' before adding '-dav-'; do not leave the 't' attached.

quiz.question: Vaikystėje aš kasdien ___ (plaukti) upėje.
quiz.explanation: Regular repeated past action for 'aš' is formed by replacing -ti with -davau (plaukti -> plaukdavau).

quiz.question: Mano močiutė kiekvieną sekmadienį ___ (kepti) gardžius blynus.
quiz.explanation: Habitual past action in the 3rd person takes the suffix -davo.

quiz.question: Mes mokykloje dažnai ___ (dainuoti) šią liaudies dainą.
quiz.explanation: The frequentative past 1st person plural (mes) ending is -davome (dainuoti -> dainuodavome).

quiz.question: Ar jūs anksčiau dažnai ___ (keliauti) traukiniu?
quiz.explanation: The 2nd person plural (jūs) frequentative past takes the ending -davote (keliauti -> keliaudavote).

tip: The frequentative past is completely regular! Just take ANY infinitive, drop '-ti', and add the '-dav-' stem endings: -davau, -davai, -davo, -davome, -davote, -davo.

title: Future Tense and Conditional Mood
subtitle: Talking about future plans and expressing polite or hypothetical wishes
keyPoint: The future tense inserts -s- before person endings, while the conditional mood uses the suffix -tų- with personal suffixes.

useCases.label: Hypothetical Conditions
useCases.example: Jeigu turėčiau laiko, eičiau į kiną.

examples.en: Aš mielai išgerčiau kavos su pienu.
Jei lis lietus, mes liktume namuose.

mistakes.note: Third-person future never takes personal endings like -i; it always ends in the bare stem with -s.
Use conditional -čiau and -tų forms for polite desires and hypothetical conditions rather than bare future.
The standard first-person plural conditional ending in Lithuanian is -tume (or colloquially -tumėme), not -tumėm.

quiz.question: Rytoj mes visi ___ naują filmą.
quiz.explanation: 'Rytoj' (tomorrow) and 'mes' require the 1st person plural future tense ending -sime.

quiz.question: Ar jūs ___ man paduoti druską?
quiz.explanation: Polite requests use the conditional form; for 'jūs', the ending is -tumėte.

quiz.question: Jei jis turėtų pinigų, jis ___ naują mašiną.
quiz.explanation: In hypothetical conditional clauses, the 3rd person takes the -tų conditional marker.

quiz.question: Aš manau, kad jis greitai ___ namo.
quiz.explanation: The 3rd person future of 'grįžti' (to return) is formed by adding -s to the infinitive stem: grįš.

tip: In third person, Lithuanian future verbs never add a personal suffix: the stem ending with -s (e.g., bus, dirbs, skaitys) serves for both singular and plural subjects.

title: Reflexive Particle Placement and Infixing
subtitle: Mastering when reflexive -si stays at the end and when it hops into the middle
keyPoint: The reflexive particle is attached at the end of simple verbs (-s/-si), but moves between the prefix and the root when a prefix is added.

mistakes.note: First person singular reflexive ends in -uosi, never add an extra -u after -si.
When a prefix like ap- is present, -si- must be placed between the prefix and verb root.
Negative prefix ne- acts as a prefix, so -si- infixes right after 'ne-' (ne-si-moko).

quiz.question: Kada tu ryte ___ iš lovos?
quiz.explanation: The 2nd person singular ('tu') reflexive present of 'keltis' is 'keliesi'.

quiz.question: Mes vakar vakare ___ su senais draugais.
quiz.explanation: Prefix 'su-' pulls the reflexive particle into an infix: su + si + tikome = susitikome.

quiz.question: Jie visai ___ šia sunkia tema.
quiz.explanation: With the negative prefix ne-, -si- is placed between ne- and the stem: ne-si-domi.

quiz.question: Vaikai kieme linksmai ___ kamuoliu.
quiz.explanation: Caution: playing games takes the non-reflexive verb 'žaisti' (žaidžia kamuoliu), not reflexive.

tip: Whenever you add ANY prefix — including the simple negative 'ne-' — the reflexive marker jumps immediately between that prefix and the root: ne-si-barti, pa-si-imti.

title: Verbal Aspect and Spatial Prefixes
subtitle: Distinguishing ongoing processes from completed actions using directional prefixes
keyPoint: Lithuanian uses prefixes like pa-, nu-, iš-, and su- to convert imperfective process verbs into perfective completed actions and specify direction.

useCases.label: Completed Action
useCases.example: Aš jau perskaičiau šią įdomią knygą.

examples.en: Ar jau parašei šį svarbų laišką?

mistakes.note: Use unprefixed imperfective verbs with duration expressions like 'tris valandas'.

mistakes.wrong: Aš jau skaičiau knygą iki galo.
mistakes.right: Aš jau perskaičiau knygą iki galo.
mistakes.note: Completing an action to the end requires a perfective prefix like per-.

mistakes.wrong: Mes valgome visą tortą per minutę.
mistakes.right: Mes suvalgėme visą tortą per minutę.
mistakes.note: Accomplishment in a set time limit ('per minutę') requires a perfective verb form.

quiz.question: Vakar aš tris valandas ___ naują romaną.
quiz.explanation: 'Tris valandas' denotes duration without completion, requiring the imperfective form 'skaičiau'.

quiz.question: Ar tu jau ___ visą šiltą pieną?
quiz.explanation: 'Išgerti' indicates drinking completely to completion (eating/drinking up).

quiz.question: Mes pagaliau ___ visus sunkios užduoties darbus.
quiz.explanation: 'Pagaliau' (at last) signals the successful completion of an action, requiring the prefix pa-.

quiz.question: Traukinys ką tik ___ iš stoties.
quiz.explanation: Movement out from a point uses the spatial/perfective prefix iš- ('išvažiavo').

tip: When a sentence has duration phrases like 'dvi valandas' (for two hours), use unprefixed verbs; when it has time-frame phrases like 'per dvi valandas' (in two hours), use a prefix.

title: Active Participles Across Tenses
subtitle: Forming and declining verbal adjectives that describe subjects performing actions
keyPoint: Active participles agree with nouns in gender, number, and case, formed with distinct suffixes: present (-ąs/-iąs/-intis), past (-ęs), and future (-siąs).

examples.en: Vaikai, skaitę šią pasaką, viską atsimena.

mistakes.note: Participles modifying nouns must agree in case; accusative masculine requires -antį, not nominative -antis.
Participles agree in gender; for feminine nominative past active, use -usi instead of masculine -ęs.
Mergaitės is feminine plural accusative, so the participle must be einančias, not masculine einančius.

quiz.question: Parke sutikome garsiai ___ mergaitę.
quiz.explanation: The noun 'mergaitę' is feminine singular accusative, so the present active participle must be 'dainuojančią'.

quiz.question: Visi mokiniai, gerai ___ namų darbus, gavo dešimtukus.
quiz.explanation: 'Mokiniai' is masculine plural nominative; the past active participle nominative plural ending is -ę (padarę).

quiz.question: Lietuvoje yra daug žmonių, ___ keliomis kalbomis.
quiz.explanation: 'Daug žmonių' requires the genitive plural form; the genitive plural active participle is 'kalbančių'.

quiz.question: Aš mačiau draugą, vakar ___ iš Vilniaus.
quiz.explanation: 'Draugą' is masculine singular accusative; past active participle accusative singular is 'grįžusį'.

tip: For present active participles used attributively before nouns, modern Lithuanian prefers the -antis / -anti nominative endings over archaic -ąs / -anti forms.

title: Passive Participles and Neuter Predicates
subtitle: Forming passive constructions and expressing impersonal rules or observations
keyPoint: Passive participles use -mas (present) and -tas (past), while neuter forms in -ma and -ta create impersonal predicate sentences.

useCases.label: Standard Passive Voice
useCases.example: Šis namas buvo pastatytas prieš šimtą metų.

examples.en: Ši graži knyga yra parašyta mano draugo.
Visi svarbūs laiškai jau buvo išsiųsti.

mistakes.note: 'Durys' (door) is a feminine plural noun in Lithuanian (pluralia tantum), so the participle must be feminine plural 'uždarytos'.
Impersonal expressions referring to infinitive actions take the neuter ending -ma/-ta, not masculine -mas.
Lithuanian marks the passive agent with the simple genitive case (tėvo), never with a preposition like 'nuo'.

quiz.question: Šis senas tiltas buvo ___ praėjusiame amžiuje.
quiz.explanation: 'Tiltas' is masculine singular nominative, requiring masculine past passive participle 'pastatytas'.

quiz.question: Bibliotekoje kalbėti garsiai yra griežtai ___.
quiz.explanation: Impersonal predicates describing verbal actions ('kalbėti') require the neuter form ending in -ma.

quiz.question: Kambario langai visą dieną buvo ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Langai' is masculine plural nominative; the agreeing past passive participle is 'uždaryti'.

quiz.question: Ši nauja daina dabar dažnai ___ per radiją.
quiz.explanation: 'Daina' is feminine singular; the present passive participle is 'grojama'.

tip: To specify WHO performed the action in a passive sentence, use the simple Genitive case with no preposition: e.g., 'knyga parašyta autoriaus' (the book was written by the author).

title: Definite (Pronominal) Adjectives
subtitle: Specifying unique, generic, or definite entities with long forms
keyPoint: Definite adjectives fuse personal pronouns onto standard adjectival stems to single out a specific item or form a fixed classification.

cells: Specific item or fixed taxonomic category

useCases.label: Proper Names and Titles
useCases.example: Vytautas Didysis valdė Lietuvos Didžiąją Kunigaikštystę.

useCases.label: Taxonomic Categories
useCases.example: Baltasis gandras yra Lietuvos nacionalinis paukštis.

examples.en: Kur yra senoji Vilniaus universiteto biblioteka?
Mano mažasis brolis šiandien pradeda lankyti mokyklą.

mistakes.note: Use definite forms for biological species and established scientific terminology.
Historical epithets and royal titles require the definite pronominal adjective.

mistakes.wrong: Noriu pirkti tą raudoną mašiną, o ne mėlyną.
mistakes.right: Noriu pirkti tą raudonąją mašiną, o ne mėlynąją.
mistakes.note: When explicitly contrasting specific identifiable objects with demonstratives, prefer the definite form.

quiz.question: Vandenyne plaukioja didžiulis ___ banginis.
quiz.explanation: The blue whale as a biological species name requires the masculine nominative definite form 'mėlynasis'.

quiz.question: Mes gyvename tame ___ name gatvės gale.
quiz.explanation: Preposition 'tame' (locative masculine) demands the corresponding locative masculine definite ending '-ajame'.

quiz.question: Raudonoji aikštė yra Maskvoje, o ___ jūra – rytuose.
quiz.explanation: Geographical sea names are feminine ('jūra') and take the feminine definite form 'Juodoji'.

quiz.question: Kur dingsta visi ___ paukščiai rudenį?
quiz.explanation: Plural masculine nominative definite form for classifying a group is 'mažieji'.

tip: Think of the suffix '-sis' / '-ji' as the English definite article 'the' permanently glued onto the end of the adjective.

title: Converbs: Pusdalyvis vs Padalyvis
subtitle: Expressing concurrent secondary actions with shared vs different subjects
keyPoint: Use pusdalyvis (-damas) when the secondary action shares the main clause subject, and padalyvis (-ant / -us) when subjects differ or action is impersonal.

useCases.label: Same Subject (Pusdalyvis)
useCases.example: Eidamas namo, Jonas sutiko seną draugą.

useCases.label: Different Subject (Padalyvis Pres.)
useCases.example: Lietui lyjant, mes sėdėjome jaukioje kavinėje.

examples.en: Eidamas namo, Jonas sutiko seną draugą.
Lietui lyjant, visi skubėjo pasislėpti po stogu.
Saulei nusileidus, keliautojai pasiekė kalnų kaimelį.
Gerdama karštą arbatą, mergina skaitė knygą.

mistakes.right: Man einant į kambarį, telefonas suskambėjo.
mistakes.note: The phone was not walking. When the subjects differ, use padalyvis with a dative agent ('man einant').

mistakes.wrong: Gerdamas kavą, man patinka žiūrėti pro langą.
mistakes.right: Gerdamas kavą, aš mėgstu žiūrėti pro langą.
mistakes.note: Pusdalyvis needs a nominative subject. Rephrase impersonal constructions like 'man patinka' to 'aš mėgstu'.
The subject of a padalyvis construction must stand in the dative case ('lietui'), not nominative.

quiz.question: ___ gatve, mergaitė pastebėjo mažą kačiuką.
quiz.explanation: The subject 'mergaitė' performs both running and noticing, so feminine singular pusdalyvis 'bėgdama' is required.

quiz.question: Tėvui ___, vaikai pradėjo ruošti pietus.
quiz.explanation: The father is in dative ('tėvui') and the main subject is 'vaikai'; different subjects in prior time require padalyvis 'grįžus'.

quiz.question: Klausydamasis muzikos, Andrius ___ laišką.
quiz.explanation: A pusdalyvis modifies a conjugated finite verb agreeing with the main subject 'Andrius rašė'.

quiz.question: Saulei ___, visa gamta pabunda naujai dienai.
quiz.explanation: Dative subject 'saulei' with an ongoing concurrent event needs present padalyvis 'tekant'.

tip: Ask: 'Is the actor doing both things?' If yes, reach for '-damas / -dama'. If no, reach for padalyvis and put that actor into dative.

title: Evidential Participles and Indirect Discourse
subtitle: Expressing hearsay, reported speech, and narrative detachment
keyPoint: Lithuanian marks reported speech and unverified hearsay (evidentiality) by replacing finite conjugated verbs with active participles.

useCases.label: Reported Hearsay
useCases.example: Girdėjau, kad kaimynai parduodą savo didelį namą.

useCases.label: Indirect Speech Complement
useCases.example: Policija pranešė vagį jau pabėgus į užsienį.

useCases.label: Folklore Narrative Tone
useCases.example: Senais laikais čia stovėjusi didelė galinga pilis.

examples.en: Girdėjau, kad kaimynai parduodą savo didelį namą.
Sakoma, kad ministras rytoj atsistatydinsiąs iš pareigų.
Senelė pasakojo ten kadaise buvus gilų ežerą.
Žmonės kalba jį laimėjus didelį prizą loterijoje.
Jis tvirtina nieko nežinąs apie šį slaptą planą.

mistakes.wrong: Jis sakė, kad jis yra nekaltas.
mistakes.note: In advanced literary and journalistic style, oblique participial clauses ('esąs') replace clunky 'kad jis yra' structures.

mistakes.wrong: Girdėjau, kad jie laimėjo (when signaling strong skepticism).
mistakes.note: Use accusative + padalyvis/participle to emphasize that the speaker does not personally vouch for the truth.
Participles in evidential constructions must agree in gender with the subject (feminine 'ateisianti' for 'mergina').

quiz.question: Liudininkas teigė matęs įtariamąjį, tačiau tas tvirtina nieko ___.
quiz.explanation: The male subject ('tas') claiming hearsay innocence requires masculine past active participle 'nematęs'.

quiz.question: Girdėjome direktorių greitai ___ iš šių pareigų.
quiz.explanation: Indirect discourse with accusative subject ('direktorių') in future reference takes future padalyvis 'pasitrauksiant'.

quiz.question: Pasakose pasakojama tolimoje karalystėje ___ karalius.
quiz.explanation: Traditional narrative evidential style uses masculine past participle 'gyvenęs' for the masculine subject 'karalius'.

quiz.question: Ji teisinosi visą dieną sunkiai ___ biure.
quiz.explanation: Nominative feminine subject 'ji' takes the nominative feminine past active participle 'dirbusi'.

tip: Evidential participles allow Lithuanian speakers to disclaim liability: using 'jis padaręs' instead of 'jis padarė' protects the reporter from libel.

title: Idiosyncratic Case Government with Complex Prepositions
subtitle: Navigating multi-case shifts with po, už, and prieš
keyPoint: Prepositions like 'po', 'už', and 'prieš' assign different cases (genitive, accusative, or instrumental) based strictly on spatial, temporal, or reciprocal meaning.

cells: ačiū už dovaną (thanks for the gift)

useCases.label: Temporal Sequence ('po' + Gen)
useCases.example: Po sunkios darbo dienos noriu tik pailsėti.

useCases.label: Spatial Position ('po' + Instr)
useCases.example: Šuo ramiai miega po dideliu mediniu stalu.

useCases.label: Exchange or Benefit ('už' + Acc)
useCases.example: Mes sumokėjome didelę kainą už šį butą.

examples.en: Po sunkios darbo dienos noriu tik pailsėti.
Šuo ramiai miega po dideliu mediniu stalu.
Mes sumokėjome didelę kainą už šį butą.
Prieš svarbų susirinkimą visi vadovai jaudinosi.

mistakes.note: Temporal 'po' (meaning 'after') always requires Genitive, never Accusative.
Spatial 'under' requires the Instrumental case ('po kuo?'), even though 'lova' looks similar, ensure instrumental inflection.
'Už' in expressions of gratitude, payment, or representation demands the Accusative case.

quiz.question: Padėk lagaminą po ___ miegamajame.
quiz.explanation: Spatial 'under' takes the instrumental; feminine singular instrumental of 'lova' is 'lova' (accented differently from nominative).

quiz.question: Mes grįšime namo tik po ___ pabaigos.
quiz.explanation: Temporal 'po' (after) governs the genitive case, hence 'koncerto'.

quiz.question: Kiek tu sumokėjai už šį naują ___?
quiz.explanation: Preposition 'už' indicating purchase or exchange strictly governs the accusative case ('dviratį').

quiz.question: Kariai drąsiai kovojo už savo tėvynės ___.
quiz.explanation: 'Kovoti už' (fight for) dictates the accusative case ('laisvę').

tip: Mnemonic: 'Po' + Time = Genitive ('po laiko'). 'Po' + Location underneath = Instrumental ('po stalu').

title: Diminutive Suffixation and Semantic Nuances
subtitle: Modulating intimacy, tenderness, and politeness through morphology
keyPoint: Lithuanian diminutives employ a vast tier of suffixes (-elis, -ytis, -iukas, -utėlis) not merely for physical size, but to encode emotional warmth, empathy, and social mitigation.

useCases.label: Emotional Warmth in Speech
useCases.example: Mano mieloji mamytė išvirė skanios sriubos.

examples.en: Mano mieloji mamytė išvirė skanios sriubos.
Ar galėtum paduoti tą puodelį arbatėlės?

mistakes.wrong: Palaukite vieną minutę! (in polite customer service)
mistakes.note: Unsuffixed commands can sound abrupt; diminutives soften everyday transactional requests.
To convey an affective, pure adjectival quality, use adjectival diminutive '-utėlis', not noun suffixes.
Native speakers almost universally prefer 'šuniukas' or 'kačiukas' when referencing juvenile or beloved pets.

quiz.question: Prašau, įpilkite man nors vieną lašelį šiltos ___.
quiz.explanation: Polite hospitality requests take genitive diminutive forms like 'vandenėlio' to sound courteous and welcoming.

quiz.question: Koks mielas ir švelnus tas tavo mažasis ___!
quiz.explanation: The standard affectionate diminutive for a kitten or cute cat is the -iukas derivative 'kačiukas'.

quiz.question: Po pirties kūdikio veidelis buvo visiškai ___.
quiz.explanation: The adjective suffix '-utėlis' conveys delicate sensory intensity ('delicately, completely red').

quiz.question: Užeikite į mūsų jaukų ___ miško pakraštyje.
quiz.explanation: Accusative singular of masculine diminutive 'namelis' governed by 'į' is 'namelį'.

tip: Lithuanian uses diminutives far beyond English 'baby talk'; they are indispensable tools of politeness and emotional tact in adult daily life.
